content.p: Wo Shing Wo is one of the triad societies that the South China Morning Post and Hong Kong Free Press name among the city's leading or best-known gangs, alongside Sun Yee On and 14K. A senior Hong Kong anti-triad detective told a Court of First Instance trial in October 2009 that the society was active in Kowloon West, running underground casinos and dealing in drugs, piracy, extortion and vice. Nearly everything known about the group in public comes from police briefings, anonymous police sources and press reports. Convictions of individual members exist, but none of the court outcomes described below is a finding about the whole society.

Its story runs through five decades of newspaper archives: a billiard-hall killing in 1975, minibus protection rackets, a scandal over a banquet that touched the race for the city's top political job, a cleaver attack on a newspaper editor, and a series of gang clashes and police raids since 2020. This account follows those episodes in order and says who made each claim.
content.h2: What the society is said to be
content.p: Triad societies trace themselves to the 17th century, when the Hung Mun brotherhood formed to overthrow the Qing dynasty, according to the South China Morning Post. After the Communist Party took power in 1949, many gangs fled to Hong Kong, which then came to be regarded as the triad capital. The paper reported that police counted some 60 gangs in the 1960s, and that new members were expected to swear the "36 oaths".

The officer who testified in 2009, Senior Detective Inspector Cheung Man-shing of the police criminal intelligence bureau, described the way such societies are organised. Lowest were "ordinary members" who had undergone a ceremony, and those "hanging the blue lantern" who had not. Above them sat office bearers such as the "red pole", responsible for operations, and the "white paper fan", responsible for administration and ceremonies. Faction leaders were called "big brothers", and the top leader "grandfather". He said triad members usually stayed silent when questioned under caution but spoke freely off the record, especially about rivals. He gave the police count of triad-related cases for the previous year as 2,378, of which 648 involved woundings and serious assaults.

The South China Morning Post said in 2010 that Wo Shing Wo had Tsuen Wan as its traditional stronghold and had extended its influence to Tsim Sha Tsui and Mong Kok. Police told the paper its extortion, drug, gambling and vice activity ran across a string of districts, from Tsuen Wan and Tsim Sha Tsui to Tai Po and Sheung Shui. The same report said its dragonhead was elected every two years.
content.h2: February 1975: two killings in two days
content.p: The earliest episode in the newspaper record involves a feud with the 14K. On the Sunday before the Post's report of 5 February 1975, members of Wo Shing Wo attacked 14K men at the Sun Hing Amusement and Billiard Saloon in Mong Kok. An 18-year-old locksmith, So Sham-pong, who was identified as a 14K member, was killed and several others were wounded. The next night a youth believed to belong to Wo Shing Wo, 18-year-old Leung Chi-wah, was found with multiple stab wounds outside a block at Tai Wo Hau Estate in Tsuen Wan, and died on the way to hospital. The paper said he was believed to have been stabbed by a group from the 14K.

Senior Kowloon police officers reportedly discussed ways to prevent a "blood-bath". A 19-year-old, Li Chik-sang, was charged with the killing of So Sham-pong. He was convicted in October 1975 and sentenced to death; in June 1976 the Governor, Sir Murray MacLehose, on the advice of the Executive Council, commuted that sentence to life imprisonment, the Post reported.

In June 2006 a police source told the South China Morning Post that Wo Shing Wo was the most active triad in the Temple Street area of Yau Ma Tei and had recruited ethnic minorities, among them Nepalis and Vietnamese. That was after a brawl in which a plain-clothes constable drew his revolver on a man still attacking one of two suspected 14K members with a knife. Police said the early inquiry showed the fight was neither premeditated nor racial in character.

In March 2010 police said a triad gang was believed to control three red minibus routes and to take at least HK$14 million a year in protection fees. A senior officer said each route involved about 30 drivers, each paying at least HK$10,000 a month. According to the paper, an alleged former dragonhead of Wo Shing Wo, a 47-year-old man surnamed Poon and known as "Broken Mouth Bun", was arrested with two women on suspicion of laundering more than HK$4 million of those fees. He had stepped down the month before. Police said they believed the extortion began in 2006, and that raids on three homes yielded about HK$1 million in gold, watches, jade and cash. The three were released on bail and nobody had been charged by the time of the report, which gives no later outcome.

In February 2012, shortly before Leung Chun-ying was elected Chief Executive, a dinner was held at a restaurant in Lau Fau Shan. According to Hong Kong Free Press, guests included Leung's election campaign chief Fanny Law, two deputies, the businessman Lew Mon-hung, several New Territories rural committee chairmen and a Yuen Long district councillor. Also there, reportedly, was Kwok Wing-hung, nicknamed "Shanghai Boy", described as an alleged former leader of Wo Shing Wo. Leung afterwards denied knowing Kwok, and said Lew had no place in his campaign office.

Casino.org, summarising Hong Kong press reports, said Kwok was believed to have been a dragonhead from 1998 to 2000, that in August 2012 he was one of 130 people picked up in a sweep of two triad gangs, said to have laundered HK$300 million, and that he stayed in jail until 2015. Those details come from that outlet alone in the pages reviewed. In December 2015 Kwok called a news conference to answer reports in Oriental Daily, which had alleged, among other things, that he blackmailed tycoons. He cancelled it at the last minute. His publicist said Kwok was "well" and "free". Posters offering HK$5 million for his whereabouts then appeared at hotels and near the Star Ferry pier; the numbers on them led to a hotel and to a woman who said she did not know him.

In November 2017, AFP reported, Kwok was arrested on suspicion of laundering more than HK$100 million. Casino.org and The Standard report that he was released on bail, did not report to a police station in April 2018 and sent word through his lawyer that he had suffered a stroke in Thailand. He was arrested at Hong Kong airport on arriving from Bangkok in November 2020. The Standard said he faced charges of conspiracy to wound with intent, conspiracy to commit criminal damage and criminal intimidation, along with jumping bail. The pages reviewed do not give a verdict on any of these charges, and he is not described here as guilty of anything.

On 26 February 2014 Kevin Lau, who had just been removed as chief editor of the newspaper Ming Pao, was attacked with a cleaver as he got out of his car in Sai Wan Ho. He suffered six wounds to the back and legs, the longest 16cm. The BBC reported that the paper offered HK$1 million for information and later raised it to HK$3 million after donations. A police source told the Post that an officer believed the attack bore the hallmarks of Wo Shing Wo, because the motorcycle first used by the attackers had been stolen in Fanling, which the officer called a stronghold of the triad. That was an officer's impression, not a finding.

Two men, Yip Kim-wah and Wong Chi-wah, were caught in mainland China and handed back to Hong Kong. At trial they said they had been tortured into confessing; the Committee to Protect Journalists reported that they had told police they were each promised HK$100,000. In August 2015 Madam Justice Esther Toh sentenced both to 19 years for causing grievous bodily harm with intent, calling it a cold-blooded crime motivated by money, and saying there was no direct evidence it was related to Lau's work as a journalist. In February 2019 the Court of Appeal rejected their appeals against sentence and described the attack as planned to a degree that "easily exceeds other cases of the same kind". Hong Kong Free Press said in 2019 that it remained unclear who was behind it. No page reviewed shows the triad being convicted of, or charged with, ordering the attack.
content.h2: Arrest sweeps and an initiation ceremony
content.p: Casino.org, reporting on the 2023 raids, said police had arrested more than 171 people in the same triad "six years" earlier. The page gives no date, place or outcome for that operation.

In November 2017 police broke up what an organised-crime officer called a rare, traditional initiation ceremony in what was reportedly a shed in Sham Shui Po, arresting four men. Images showed an altar, incense, rice wine and a meat cleaver.

In September 2020 the group's 45-year-old leader, known as "Crazy Yung", was shot in the chest by a gunman on a motorcycle in Tsim Sha Tsui and survived. The Standard said police understood the quarrel was with a former leader over a pier used for smuggling. Police raided a bar, a gambling den and a Tsuen Wan flat in the same days. In June 2021 police said they had broken up a triad bookmaking ring; Casino.org reported, citing a police source, that handwritten records showed more than US$438 million in illegal bets in four months, and that 18 people were arrested.

In June 2021 a 27-year-old man, Luk Wing, was forced to fight a series of kickboxing matches at a Tai Kok Tsui gym by dozens of Wo Shing Wo members, police said, who accused him of embezzling HK$1 million from a woman called the "big sister". He fell unconscious in his ninth match and died on 4 August. Police arrested six members, and then the alleged "big sister" and six others in a later raid in Fan Ling. Police said she did not take part but encouraged the fights. Two suspects had been charged with murder by the time of the report.

On 10 June 2022 at about 2:30 a.m. at least eight men armed with knives got out of cars and attacked three vehicles stopped at a red light on Wyndham Street, near Lan Kwai Fong. Shots were fired and three men were hurt. Police said the incident came from a long-running feud between two triad groups over illegal gambling and drugs. A force source told the Post it was between Sun Yee On and Wo Shing Wo over the uneven sharing of profits. By 28 June police had arrested 16 people, eight of them charged, but had not found the pistol. They said 1,088 people had been arrested in follow-up operations on bars, mahjong parlours and clubs.

A trial in 2022 added another strand. Three police officers, Sergeant Chiu Kwong-lam, Constable Lai Fuk-hong and Constable Fu Yu-man, were found guilty over a 2018 tip-off to the Tsuen Wan faction about a planned gambling-den raid. They had unknowingly told an undercover officer; a fourth officer was cleared.

In August 2023 police arrested 83 people in three days of raids on illegal gambling and money laundering. Casino.org reported that among them were the wife and son of an alleged senior figure of the society, whose family managed HK$68 million while declaring HK$1.6 million of income over nine years. In March 2024 police arrested at least 21 members of the two gangs after three knife attacks across Tuen Mun, Yuen Long and Tin Shui Wai, which sources said began with a dispute over a woman.
